To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) intermittent administration of cocaine to mice results in a sensitized response to a subsequent cocaine challenge, while continuous administration results in a tolerant response; (b) the changes in locomotor response are correlated with the levels of cocaine in the brain after challenge, suggesting that the changes in the response are due to dispositional factors; (c) the sensitized and the tolerant animals have the same cocaine and benzoecgonine levels in plasma and brain after challenge, which suggests that the changes

1) the locomotor stimulatory effect of a challenge dose is greater in mice that were previously treated intermittently with cocaine than in those treated continuously; 2) this difference is not due to differences in the disposition of cocaine in the brain; 3) the locomotor stimulation of cocaine in animals previously treated with cocaine is positively correlated with their cocaine levels in the brain.

in mice, the locomotor stimulation by a challenge dose of 10 mg/kg cocaine was greater in animals treated with cocaine intermittently than in animals treated continuously, and that there was no correlation between the brain cocaine levels and the locomotor stimulation in the continuously treated animals, whereas there was a positive relationship in the intermittently treated animals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a possible relationship between cocaine disposition and its behavioral effect.
the relationship between the disposition of cocaine in the brain and the behavioral response to cocaine in animals chronically treated with the drug.
the effects of chronic cocaine treatment on its locomotor stimulant properties and its disposition in brain and plasma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the changes in the behavioral effect of cocaine after continuous or intermittent administration of the drug are not related to the dispositional effects of the drug in the brain.
in these experiments there is a positive correlation between brain cocaine concentration and locomotor stimulation by cocaine, but that in chronic experiments the correlation is not always present.
the changes in the brain disposition of cocaine are not the sole cause of the changes in the behavioral response to the challenge dose of cocaine.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in chronic cocaine administration in mice, the changes in locomotor response to a subsequent challenge are not accounted for simply by the cocaine disposition.

in the mouse the changes in cocaine disposition are not a factor in the changes in the behavioral effects of cocaine after continuous or intermittent administration, whereas after daily administration for 2 or more days there is a dispositional factor that is correlated with the behavioral effects.

the locomotor response of mice to cocaine challenge after chronic intermittent or continuous treatment is not related to dispositional effects, whereas in animals treated daily with cocaine, there is a dispositional component to the locomotor response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in chronic treatment experiments the changes in locomotor stimulation are not accounted for solely by dispositional effects.

chronic treatment with cocaine, either by intermittent or by continuous administration, does not result in differences in cocaine disposition, but that the differences in locomotor stimulation between these groups are due to different mechanisms.

the changes in the disposition of cocaine in the brain do not account for the changes in locomotor response to cocaine in mice treated for 2-4 weeks with cocaine by either intermittent or continuous administration.
